An Information-Space Perspective to
Scene Graph Sufficiency for Robotic Task Planning

Başak Sakçak Affiliation: Dept. of Advanced Computing Sciences, Maastricht University, the Netherlands (basak.sakcak@maastrichtuniversity.nl)    Francesco Verdoja ††thanks: F. Verdoja was supported by the Research Council of Finland (decision 354909) during this work. Affiliation: School of Electrical Engineering, Aalto University, Finland (francesco.verdoja@aalto.fi)
Abstract

Planning in complex environments requires task specifications grounded in representations that capture objects, relations, and affordances; scene graphs meet this need, but their size in large environments hinders efficient planning. While task-aware pruning and hierarchical abstractions have been explored, a general, task-centric formalization of what constitutes a sufficient scene graph for planning remains open. This paper provides such a formalization by modeling planning over scene graphs within an information-spaces framework through the definition of scene graph transition systems and relevant action semantics for navigation and manipulation. We then introduce derived scene graphs via information mappings that merge and prune nodes and induce quotient transition systems augmented with motion primitives to capture higher-level actions over merged graph nodes. Sufficiency is characterized by two conditions: (i) the information mapping yields a deterministic quotient, and (ii) the task is well-posed over derived traces, ensuring plans found on the derived model are feasible on the maximal system. We illustrate the framework using a task over an example environment, showing both sufficient and insufficient reduced scene graphs.

I Introduction

Robots typically achieve desired behavior in the physical world by planning sequences of actions in advance. Planning, in turn, requires a model that captures the objects in the physical world, their attributes, and the relations and affordances that constrain possible robot actions. Over this model, the desired behavior can be specified and effects of the robot actions can be evaluated. Planning directly on raw world models (e.g., dense metric maps or point clouds) becomes quickly intractable, while purely symbolic descriptions lack the contextual detail needed to ensure realizable, context-appropriate plans.

Scene graphs have emerged as a compelling middle ground: by modeling environments as hierarchical graphs of spatial entities and their relations, they provide a semantically rich abstraction that grounds planning in the actual state of the world, and can be constructed online from sensor data to autonomously instantiate planning domains [1, 2]. Yet real environments induce large scene graphs, significantly increasing planning complexity [3]. Existing scene-graph planning approaches show that smaller, task-relevant graphs improve planning [2, 4, 5, 3], but they largely rely on heuristics or Large Language Models (LLMs), offering empirical rather than principled guarantees about preserving plan existence and feasibility. This paper focuses on the complementary formal aspect of determining what information a derived scene graph must preserve so that plans found on it correspond to feasible plans on the maximal scene graph.

In parallel with this scene-graph literature, a line of work on information spaces studies what encoding of information given as a robot’s interaction history of action-observation pairs is needed for tasks to remain solvable [6, 7]. However, a gap exists between this formalism and its application to concrete problems. Borrowing ideas from [6], we address the problem of “simplifying” a scene graph representation and propose a formal structure over which questions about the sufficiency of a simplified scene graph in terms of determining a plan feasible for the original representation can be understood in a precise way.

The main contribution of this paper is a framework for reasoning about sufficiency of scene graphs for robotic task planning. First we extend the framework in [6] and introduce conditions under which an internal representation is sufficient for planning purposes, and when motion primitives are used. Then, we connect these conditions to planning over scene graphs. We define scene graph transition systems, involving navigation and manipulation actions. Then, we formalize derived scene graphs as quotient models induced by many-to-one information mappings, with motion primitives accounting for high-level actions. We then provide conditions under which plans found over derived systems remain feasible for the maximal system.

II Related Literature

Mapping semantic information enables complex planning in many robotics domains, from autonomous driving to mobile manipulation. Beyond augmenting traditional 2D/3D maps, 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) have emerged as metric-semantic representations whose nodes denote spatial concepts (rooms, objects) and edges encode relations (inclusion, adjacency) [8, 9]. They provide memory-efficient, perception-driven semantic understanding and have been demonstrated in real-time operation on robots, e.g., Hydra [1, 8]. Extensions broaden semantic content with open-vocabulary features (ConceptGraphs [10]) and address long-term mapping [11, 12].

Scene graphs are increasingly being adopted as representations for task and motion planning (TAMP). Two main directions appear: leveraging scene-graph structure and hierarchy to build planning domains or to plan iteratively across levels [2, 13, 14, 15], and using large language models (LLMs) that consume the scene graph as context [4, 15]. Because planning on full graphs is complex, most of these methods decompose them through either: high-to-low abstraction planning that focuses on nodes relevant to the current plan [13, 15]; heuristics that compress dense subgraphs (e.g., aggregating equivalent nodes) [2, 3]; and iterative subgraph expansion, sometimes guided by LLMs [4]. Some existing methods (e.g., [3]), provide guarantees in specific symbolic planning settings, while many heuristic, learned, and LLM-guided reductions are evaluated empirically. Complementary to these methods, we provide a formal framework for determining when a derived scene graph induced by pruning (but also merging) preserves information needed for planning.

More broadly, solving robotic planning problems requires choosing a model of the robot–environment dynamics, which also determines plan existence and feasibility in the original system. A key line of work asks what information from action–observation histories must be retained for tasks to be solvable: histories are mapped to information states (equivalence classes), yielding minimally sufficient quotients that can simulate history-based policies [6, 16, 7, 17]. These ideas align with formal methods, where abstractions preserve properties via simulation and refinement [18]. In TAMP literature, PDDL [19] abstracts geometric and differential constraints into predicates and discrete actions that must be grounded by motion planning; because even few objects and predicates induce large state spaces, structure-preserving simplifications are pursued [20, 21].

Together, these works show that scene graphs are useful planning representations but abstraction is necessary for scalability. However, existing scene-graph planning approaches typically evaluate abstractions empirically. In contrast, information-space and formal-abstraction methods investigate whether a representation preserves the necessary task-related information for planning or plan execution. Here, we bridge these directions by casting scene-graph reduction as an information mapping and by giving conditions under which a derived scene graph is sufficient for planning.

III Sufficient Models for Planning

III-B Planner Perspective

A robot embedded in and interacting with an environment is modeled as two coupled transition systems, named internal and external systems in [6]. The external system corresponds to the physical environment, including the robot body, and the internal system represents the perspective of a decision maker. Let 𝒳=(X,U,f){\mathcal{X}}=(X,U,f) be a transition system representing the external system, in which, XX and UU are the external state and action spaces, f:X×U→Xf:X\times U\rightarrow X is a state transition function such that f⁡(x,u)f(x,u) is the state reached after taking action uu at state xx. In this work, we extend the framework presented in [6] by introducing the planner perspective for the internal system. Given a task description, we consider a planner that systematically explores the space of all finite sequences of actions over a given model and determines one that satisfies the given task. Tasks are modeled over the finite external system traces.

Definition 1 (Task)

Given 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, letΩ𝒳\Omega_{\mathcal{X}} denote the set of all traces of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}. A task TT for an external system 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} is the subset T⊆Ω𝒳T\subseteq\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}.

Given a task, a plan is determined so that the robot exhibits the desired behavior, in which case it is called a feasible plan for task TT. In this work, we focus on plans that are represented as a sequence of actions, as this is typical for many planning problems, including many for which scene graphs have been proposed, e.g., [2, 4].

Definition 2 (Feasible plan for TT)

Given an external system 𝒳=(X,U,f){\mathcal{X}}=(X,U,f) initialized at x1∈Xx_{1}\in X, let ωu~​(x1)=(x1,u1,x2,…,uN−1,xN)∈Ω𝒳\omega_{\tilde{u}(x_{1})}=(x_{1},u_{1},x_{2},\dots,u_{N-1},x_{N})\in\Omega_{\mathcal{X}} be a trace corresponding to a plan u~​(x1)=(u1,u2,…,uN−1)\tilde{u}(x_{1})=(u_{1},u_{2},\dots,u_{N-1}) of some length N−1N-1. A plan u~​(x1)\tilde{u}(x_{1}) is called a feasible plan for TT if ωu~​(x1)∈T\omega_{\tilde{u}(x_{1})}\in T.

Given a task TT for an external system 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, the objective of a planner is to determine a feasible plan for TT. However, typically, the planner is given a model of the external system over which also the task TT is transcribed. Let ℳ=(XM,U,fM){\mathcal{M}}=(X_{M},U,f_{M}) be a model of the external system, in which XMX_{M} is the set of states, UU is the set of actions, and fMf_{M} is a state transition function. Given ℳ{\mathcal{M}}, an initial state x1∈XMx_{1}\in X_{M}, and a task TM⊆ΩℳT_{M}\subseteq\Omega_{\mathcal{M}}, a planner systematically explores XMX_{M} and the space of action sequences consistent with ℳ{\mathcal{M}}. A solution is found if a particular sequence of actions results in a trace that belongs in TMT_{M}. Two questions arise: (i) can the task TT be expressed over the traces of ℳ{\mathcal{M}}? (ii) is a plan feasible for TMT_{M} also feasible for TT? These questions are addressed in the following subsection.

III-C Sufficient Models for Planning

To determine conditions under which feasible plans determined by a planner using a particular model are feasible for the external system as well, we focus on models that are quotient systems derived from an external system 𝒳=(X,U,f){\mathcal{X}}=(X,U,f) through a labeling function κ:X→XM{\kappa}:X\rightarrow X_{M} named an information mapping (I-map). Given κ{\kappa}, the quotient of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} by κ{\kappa} is the transition system ℳ:=(X/κ,U,f/κ){\mathcal{M}}:=(X/{\kappa},U,f/{\kappa}). At the highest level, a model of the external system is the external system itself, that is, κ{\kappa} is a bijection and ℳ=𝒳{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{X}}. However, in most cases this model is prohibitive for search, and we are interested in determining a “simpler” one as a quotient system obtained by a many-to-one mapping κ{\kappa}. A crucial requirement on this quotient system is that it should still allow determining a feasible plan for task TT. Note that the quotient system may not be deterministic as this depends on the selected labeling function κ{\kappa}. Suppose for all x,s,x′,s′∈Xx,s,x^{\prime},s^{\prime}\in X and all u∈Uu\in U, the following holds:

κ⁡(x)=κ⁡(s)∧x′=f⁡(x,u)∧s′=f⁡(s,u)⟹\displaystyle{\kappa}(x)={\kappa}(s)\,\land\,x^{\prime}=f(x,u)\,\land\,s^{\prime}=f(s,u)\implies (1)
κ⁡(x′)=κ⁡(s′).\displaystyle{\kappa}(x^{\prime})={\kappa}(s^{\prime}).

Then, the resulting quotient system (X/κ,U,f/κ)(X/{\kappa},U,f/{\kappa}) is deterministic as well [6]. A labeling function κ{\kappa} is called sufficient if it satisfies the implication given in (1). Thus, if κ{\kappa} is sufficient, the labels can be uniquely determined when limited to the quotient system.

When using a derived system for planning, it is natural to ask whether the task can still be expressed over the traces of this new system. Given 𝒳=(X,U,f){\mathcal{X}}=(X,U,f) and a derived system ℳ=(XM,U,fM):=𝒳/κ{\mathcal{M}}=(X_{M},U,f_{M}):={\mathcal{X}}/{\kappa}, let Ω𝒳\Omega_{\mathcal{X}} and Ωℳ\Omega_{{\mathcal{M}}} be the corresponding sets of traces. Furthermore, let cκ:Ω𝒳→Ωℳc_{\kappa}:\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}\rightarrow\Omega_{{\mathcal{M}}} be a mapping, named I-map condenser, under which

(x1,u1,…,xN)↦(κ⁡(x1),u1,…,κ⁡(xN)).(x_{1},u_{1},\dots,x_{N})\mapsto({\kappa}(x_{1}),u_{1},\dots,{\kappa}(x_{N})). (2)

A task TT is called well-posed under cκc_{{\kappa}} if cκ(cκ(T))−1=Tc_{{\kappa}}{{}^{-1}}(c_{{\kappa}}(T))=T [22]. Informally, well-posedness means that a task expressed over Ω𝒳\Omega_{\mathcal{X}} can similarly be expressed over Ωℳ\Omega_{{\mathcal{M}}} without losing any task-related information. Thus, because task accomplishment information can be determined solely by the derived system traces without ambiguities, we can say that the derived system is rich enough for planning purposes.

The following definition combines two requirements for a useful model. Sufficiency of κ{\kappa} guarantees deterministic behavior of the model transitions and sufficiency of cκc_{\kappa}, while well-posedness guarantees that task satisfaction is determined completely by the model trace.

Definition 3 (Sufficient model for planning)

Given an external system 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}, a model ℳ=𝒳/κ{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{X}}/{\kappa} is called sufficient for planning for task TT if (i) κ{\kappa} is sufficient, and (ii) the task TT is well-posed under cκc_{\kappa}.

III-D Motion Primitives

The quotient structure introduced in the previous section assumes that the original and the derived system share the same set of actions. However, often a set of higher-level actions (motion primitives) that correspond to a sequence from set UU is used, typically parametrized by the system states. For example, an action such as move to a region may require executing a sequence of lower-level actions whose intermediate external states are not represented in the model. The next definition formalizes this notion.

Definition 4 (Motion primitive)

Let 𝒳=(X,U,f){\mathcal{X}}=(X,U,f) be an external system. A motion primitive σ\sigma is a mapping σ:X→U<ℕ\sigma:X\rightarrow U^{<{\mathbb{N}}} assigning to every state x∈Xx\in X a finite action sequence σ⁡(x)=(u1,…,uN)\sigma(x)=(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}). Starting from some x1=xx_{1}=x, the execution of σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) induces the finite trace

f¯​(x,σ):=(x1,u1,x2,…,uN,xN+1),\bar{f}(x,\sigma):=\left(x_{1},u_{1},x_{2},\dots,u_{N},x_{N+1}\right),

in which xi+1=f⁡(xi,ui)x_{i+1}=f(x_{i},u_{i}). The corresponding endpoint transition is ⋄f(x,σ):=xN+1.\diamond_{f}(x,\sigma):=x_{N+1}.

We can consider a set of motion primitives to be the new set of actions for the external system. Let Σ\Sigma denote the set of motion primitives. Using Σ\Sigma as the set of actions, the system restricted by the motion primitives is given by 𝒳Σ=(X,Σ,⋄f){\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}=(X,\Sigma,\diamond_{f}) and we use Ω𝒳Σ{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}} to denote its traces.

Given a sequence of actions σ~∈(Σ)N\tilde{\sigma}\in(\Sigma)^{N} for some NN, the respective trace of 𝒳Σ{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma} is given by

ωσ~=(x1,σ1,x2,σ2,…,σN,xN+1)∈Ω𝒳Σ,\omega_{\tilde{\sigma}}=(x_{1},\sigma_{1},x_{2},\sigma_{2},\dots,\sigma_{N},x_{N+1})\in\Omega_{{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}},

in which xi+1=⋄f(xi,σi)x_{i+1}={\diamond_{f}}(x_{i},\sigma_{i}), i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N. Each motion primitive σi\sigma_{i} induces a finite trace f¯​(xi,σi){\bar{f}}(x_{i},\sigma_{i}) of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}}. Hence, the corresponding trace in 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} is obtained by concatenating the subtraces induced by the individual motion primitives,

ω¯σ~=f¯(x1,σ1)f¯⌢(x2,σ2)…⌢f¯⌢(xN,σN),\bar{\omega}_{\tilde{\sigma}}={\bar{f}}(x_{1},\sigma_{1}){}^{\frown}{\bar{f}}(x_{2},\sigma_{2}){}^{\frown}\dots{}^{\frown}{\bar{f}}(x_{N},\sigma_{N}),

Since each ω¯σ~\bar{\omega}_{{\tilde{\sigma}}} is defined through its generating primitive sequence σ~{\tilde{\sigma}}, its decomposition into motion primitive induced subtraces is fixed by construction. We then define the motion-primitive condenser cMP:Ω¯𝒳Σ→Ω𝒳Σc_{\text{MP}}:\bar{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}}\rightarrow{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}} by cMP​(ω¯σ~)=ωσ~c_{\text{MP}}(\bar{\omega}_{\tilde{\sigma}})=\omega_{\tilde{\sigma}}. Since restricting the action set to motion primitives may exclude some traces of Ω𝒳\Omega_{\mathcal{X}}, we define the task considered by this restricted system as TΣ:=T∩Ω¯𝒳ΣT_{\Sigma}:=T\cap\bar{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}}.

For a set X0⊆XX_{0}\subseteq X of admissible initial states, we say that Σ\Sigma is complete for TT if ∀x1∈X0\forall x_{1}\in X_{0}, Tx1≠∅⟹(TΣ)x1≠∅T_{x_{1}}\not=\varnothing\implies(T_{\Sigma})_{x_{1}}\not=\varnothing, in which the subscript x1x_{1} denotes the respective traces beginning at x1x_{1}. If Σ\Sigma is complete for TT, then existence of feasible plan from x1x_{1} over 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} implies that there exists a feasible plan from x1x_{1} over 𝒳Σ{\mathcal{X}}_{\Sigma}.

IV Scene Graph Transition Systems

In this section, we introduce the notion of scene graph transition system as an application of the theory presented in Sec. III. When defining the scene graph, we follow the conventions used in previous work [1, 23]. We will also introduce a sample set of actions relevant to simple navigation and manipulation, similar to [2].

IV-A Scene graph representation

A scene graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) maps spatio-semantic relations among scene elements via edges EE over nodes VV. Nodes represent spatial elements (e.g., tables, robots, bedrooms) with spatial features (pose/configuration, bounding box) and semantic features (class, affordances, color). Following [1], we use five node categories: building, rooms, places, objects, and agents. A place is a region within a room obtained by space decomposition, e.g., GVD [24] or 2D polygons from meshes [2], such that each object/agent lies entirely in one place and all navigable positions within a place are path-connected. We denote building, room, place, and object, and agent node sets as VbV_{b}, VrV_{r}, VpV_{p}, VoV_{o}, and VaV_{a}, respectively. In this work, we take Va:={va}V_{a}:=\{v_{a}\}, in which vav_{a} is the node representing the robot. Many scene graphs include a 3D mesh [1] or point cloud [23] as the global spatial frame; we omit this here since it mainly supports localization and motion planning rather than abstract reasoning or task planning. We consider three types of edges, encoding inclusion, adjacency, and carrier relations, though additional relations (e.g., functional [25] or event [5]) are possible.

Definition 5 (General Inclusion Relation)

A general inclusion relation is an asymmetric and transitive binary relation denoted by ℛginc⊆V×V{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}}\subseteq V\times V. We say vjv_{j} is included in viv_{i} if (vi,vj)∈ℛginc(v_{i},v_{j})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}}. Let vsv_{s} be the root node which is the largest spatial category such that all nodes in V∖{vs}V\setminus\{v_{s}\} are included in vsv_{s}. Then, ℛginc{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}} satisfies that for any vj∈V∖{vs}v_{j}\in V\setminus\{v_{s}\} exists a vi∈Vv_{i}\in V such that (vi,vj)∈ℛginc(v_{i},v_{j})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}}.

Definition 6 (Reduced Inclusion Relation)

A reduced inclusion relation, alternatively, an inclusion relation, is a binary relation ℛinc⊆ℛginc{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{inc}}\subseteq{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}} obtained by removing from ℛginc{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}} the pairs (vi,vj)(v_{i},v_{j}) satisfying that there exists a vkv_{k} such that (vi,vk)∈ℛginc(v_{i},v_{k})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}} and (vk,vj)∈ℛginc(v_{k},v_{j})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{ginc}}.

When considering spatial elements at progressively finer resolutions (e.g., from buildings to objects), inclusion relations are used to introduce a spatial hierarchy (e.g., the robot being in a specific place). We assume each spatial element vjv_{j} to only have one parent, i.e., ∀vj∈V∖{vs},{vi∣(vi,vj)∈ℛinc}\forall v_{j}\in V\setminus\{v_{s}\},\{v_{i}\mid(v_{i},v_{j})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{inc}}\} is a singleton. Under this assumption, inclusion relations (Definition 6) form a hierarchical tree 𝒯inc=(V,ℛinc){\mathcal{T}}_{\text{inc}}=(V,{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{inc}}). For concreteness, in this paper, we use a tree with depth three, with nodes at each depth representing respectively the building (V0=VbV_{0}=V_{b}, consisting of the root node vsv_{s} alone), rooms (V1=VrV_{1}=V_{r}), places (V2=VpV_{2}=V_{p}), and objects and agents (V3=Vo∪VaV_{3}=V_{o}\cup V_{a}).

Let ℱ⁡(vp)\mathcal{F}(v_{p}) denote the free configuration space associated with a place node vp∈Vpv_{p}\in V_{p}. We assume that each ℱ⁡(vp)\mathcal{F}(v_{p}) is path connected.

Definition 7 (Adjacency Relation)

An adjacency relation is a symmetric irreflexive relation ℛadj⊆Vp×Vp{\mathcal{R}}_{{\text{adj}}}\subseteq V_{p}\times V_{p}. Two place nodes vi,vj∈Vpv_{i},v_{j}\in V_{p} are adjacent, written (vi,vj)∈ℛadj(v_{i},v_{j})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{{\text{adj}}}, if there exists a path contained in ℱ⁡(vi)∪ℱ⁡(vj)\mathcal{F}(v_{i})\cup\mathcal{F}(v_{j}), or in its closure, connecting a point in ℱ⁡(vi)\mathcal{F}(v_{i}) to a point in ℱ⁡(vj)\mathcal{F}(v_{j}).

Definition 8 (Carrier Relation)

A carrier relation is an irreflexive and acyclic relation over VaV_{a} and VoV_{o}, i.e., ℛcar⊆(Vo∪Va)×Vo{\mathcal{R}}_{{\text{car}}}\subseteq(V_{o}\cup V_{a})\times V_{o}. We say that viv_{i} is carrying vjv_{j} if (vi,vj)∈ℛcar(v_{i},v_{j})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{{\text{car}}}. The relation represents a kinematic link, in such a way that if viv_{i} moves, then vjv_{j} moves with it.

Definition 9 (Scene Graph)

A scene graph is an edge-labeled directed graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) in which E=ℛinc∪ℛadj∪ℛcarE={\mathcal{R}}_{\text{inc}}\cup{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adj}}\cup{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{car}} together with an edge labeling function ℓe:E→ℒ\ell_{e}:E\rightarrow{\mathcal{L}} that attributes each edge a label from the set ℒ={inc,adj,car}{\mathcal{L}}=\{{\text{inc}},{\text{adj}},{\text{car}}\} consistent with the relation that generated the edge.

This definition makes explicit the scene graph structure that prior works use implicitly (e.g., [1, 2, 4, 23, 26]); to our knowledge, this is the first formal statement of it. In the following, we will use E⁡(G)E(G) and V⁡(G)V(G) to denote the edges and nodes of GG, respectively. We will use (vi,vj)ℓ(v_{i},v_{j})_{\ell} to denote the label ℓ∈ℒ\ell\in{\mathcal{L}} of the edge connecting (vi,vj)(v_{i},v_{j}).

Example 1 (Scene graph)

Consider the environment ee (Fig. 1(a)) consisting of three rooms (r1r_{1}, r2r_{2}, r3r_{3}), with both r1r_{1} and r3r_{3} only adjacent to r2r_{2} (i.e., an open door exists between these rooms). Room r1r_{1} is subdivided into two places (p1p_{1}, p2p_{2}), room r2r_{2} in three places (p3p_{3}, p4p_{4}, p5p_{5}), while room r3r_{3} is composed of only one place (p6p_{6}). Places are adjacent to each other according to Fig. 1(a). Currently, p1p_{1} contains a mug mm onto a table tt, while p6p_{6} contains a desk dd and the robotic agent aa. The scene graph G1G_{1} for this environment is shown in Fig. 1(b). The spatial and semantic features of elements in Vo​(G1)V_{o}(G_{1}) (e.g., pose, bounding box, semantic class) are omitted from this example for brevity.

IV-B Scene graph transition system

Using scene graphs as its states, a robot-environment system is modeled as a deterministic transition system.

Definition 10 (Scene Graph Transition System)

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be the set of all possible scene graphs for a given robot-environment system satisfying that for any G,G′∈𝒢G,G^{\prime}\in{\mathcal{G}}, V⁡(G)=V⁡(G′)V(G)=V(G^{\prime}). A scene graph transition system is the tuple 𝒳=(𝒢,U⁡(𝒢),f){\mathcal{X}}=({\mathcal{G}},U({\mathcal{G}}),f), in which U⁡(𝒢)U({\mathcal{G}}) is the set of actions consistent with the scene graph representation and f:𝒢×U⁡(𝒢)→𝒢f:{\mathcal{G}}\times U({\mathcal{G}})\rightarrow{\mathcal{G}} is the state transition function.

To formally define the scene graph transition function, we first introduce a set of actions. Note that different sets of actions are possible depending on the scene graph representation and robot embodiment. However, we assume that all action sets are parametrized by the graph nodes and encode possible ways a robot can interact with its environment. Interactions could be for example, navigation, manipulation, and inspection. In the following, we introduce the set of actions that we will refer to in the examples used throughout the paper.

Definition 11 (Action set of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}})

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be the set of all scene graphs, let Umove​(𝒢)U_{\text{move}}({\mathcal{G}}), Upick​(𝒢)U_{\text{pick}}({\mathcal{G}}), and Uplaceon​(𝒢)U_{\text{placeon}}({\mathcal{G}}) be the sets of actions parametrized by the graph nodes such that

Umove​(𝒢)\displaystyle U_{\text{move}}({\mathcal{G}}) :={𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(vpi)∣vpi∈Vp​(𝒢)},\displaystyle:=\{\moveto(v_{p_{i}})\mid{v_{p_{i}}\in V_{p}({\mathcal{G}})}\},
Upick​(𝒢)\displaystyle U_{\text{pick}}({\mathcal{G}}) :={𝚙𝚒𝚌𝚔(voi)∣voi∈Vo​(𝒢)},\displaystyle:=\{\pick(v_{o_{i}})\mid{v_{o_{i}}\in V_{o}({\mathcal{G}})}\},
Uplaceon​(𝒢)\displaystyle U_{\text{placeon}}({\mathcal{G}}) :={𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚌𝚎𝚘𝚗(voi,voj)∣voi,voj∈Vo(𝒢)},\displaystyle:=\{\placeon(v_{o_{i}},v_{o_{j}})\mid{v_{o_{i}},v_{o_{j}}\in V_{o}({\mathcal{G}})}\},

in which Vp​(𝒢)V_{p}({\mathcal{G}}) and Vo​(𝒢)V_{o}({\mathcal{G}}) are the sets of all place nodes and object nodes, respectively. Then, the set of actions for a space of scene graphs 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} is U⁡(𝒢):=Umove​(𝒢)∪Upick​(𝒢)∪Uplaceon​(𝒢).U({\mathcal{G}}):=U_{\text{move}}({\mathcal{G}})\cup U_{\text{pick}}({\mathcal{G}})\cup U_{\text{placeon}}({\mathcal{G}}).

The set of actions given in Definition 11 are interpreted over the scene graphs in the following ways.

IV-B1 Move action

Let GG be a scene graph and let G′:=f⁡(G,𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(vp′))G^{\prime}:=f(G,\moveto(v_{p}^{\prime})). Let vpv_{p} correspond to the place the robot is in, that is, (vp,va)inc∈E⁡(G)(v_{p},v_{a})_{{\text{inc}}}\in E(G), in which vav_{a} is the node representing the robot. If (vp,vp′)a​d​j∈E⁡(G)(v_{p},v_{p^{\prime}})_{adj}\in E(G), applying the action 𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(vp′)\moveto(v_{p^{\prime}}) removes the inclusion edge (vp,va)inc(v_{p},v_{a})_{\text{inc}} and adds (vp′,va)inc(v_{p^{\prime}},v_{a})_{\text{inc}}. Similarly, for any vov_{o} satisfying that (va,vo)car∈E⁡(G)(v_{a},v_{o})_{\text{car}}\in E(G), the inclusion edge (vp,vo)inc(v_{p},v_{o})_{\text{inc}} is removed and (vp′,vo)inc(v_{p^{\prime}},v_{o})_{\text{inc}} is added. Moving an object from one place to another might change whether two places are path connected. The adjacency relations, consequently the scene graph edges, are updated accordingly with the move of an object. If (vp,vp′)a​d​j∉E⁡(G)(v_{p},v_{p^{\prime}})_{adj}\not\in E(G), (G,𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(vp′))↦G(G,\moveto(v_{p^{\prime}}))\mapsto G under ff.

IV-B2 Pick action

A pick action takes an object node as a parameter. Applying 𝚙𝚒𝚌𝚔(vo)\pick(v_{o}) action, in which vov_{o} is an object node in place vpv_{p}, adds the carrier edge (va,vo)car(v_{a},v_{o})_{\text{car}} to E⁡(G)E(G) if (vp,vo)inc,(vp,va)inc∈E⁡(G)(v_{p},v_{o})_{\text{inc}},(v_{p},v_{a})_{\text{inc}}\in E(G), that is the object oo is picked up by the robot if they are in the same place, and if the cardinality of the carrier relations the robot is in does not exceed a predefined number. Furthermore, any previous carrier edge that involves vov_{o} is removed. Otherwise, (G,𝚙𝚒𝚌𝚔(vo))↦G(G,\pick(v_{o}))\mapsto G under ff.

IV-B3 Placeon action

A 𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚌𝚎𝚘𝚗(⋅)\placeon(\cdot) action is parametrized by a pair of object nodes (oi,oj)(o_{i},o_{j}). Assume GG contains a carrier edge (va,voi)car(v_{a},v_{o_{i}})_{\text{car}}, and inclusion edges (vp,va)inc,(vp,voi)inc,(vp,voj)inc∈E⁡(G)(v_{p},v_{a})_{\text{inc}},(v_{p},v_{o_{i}})_{\text{inc}},(v_{p},v_{o_{j}})_{\text{inc}}\in E(G) for some place node vpv_{p}, i.e., the agent and both oio_{i} and ojo_{j} are in the same place. Then, applying 𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚌𝚎𝚘𝚗(voi,voj)\placeon(v_{o_{i}},v_{o_{j}}) removes the carrier edge (va,voi)car(v_{a},v_{o_{i}})_{\text{car}} from GG and adds the carrier edge (voj,voi)car(v_{o_{j}},v_{o_{i}})_{\text{car}}. Otherwise, after applying this action the state remains the same.

V Sufficient Scene Graphs for Planning

When a scene graph transition system is obtained through some perception pipeline (e.g., [1]), we consider this to be a maximal model of the external system (physical world). In this section, based on the framework introduced in Sec. III, we present a new perspective to analyze what is necessary from a scene graph given a planning task. To this end, we introduce the notions derived scene graph and derived scene graph transition system and discuss the conditions under which such a system is sufficient for planning.

V-A Derived Scene Graphs

Let 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} be the set of all possible maximal scene graphs for a given robot-environment system. We will refer to 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} as the maximal scene graph space. A derived scene graph space 𝒢der{\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}} is then the codomain of some many-to one I-map κ:𝒢→𝒢der{\kappa}:{\mathcal{G}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}. We want 𝒢der{\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}, the codomain of κ{\kappa}, to also be a set of scene graphs, i.e., its elements satisfy Definition 9.

The I-map κ{\kappa} is defined through merge and prune operations over the elements of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}. Specifically, we consider merging nodes in VpV_{p} and VrV_{r} (nodes corresponding to places and rooms) and pruning nodes in VoV_{o} (nodes corresponding to objects). To merge nodes of GG, we define two equivalence relations respectively between the nodes in VpV_{p} and in VrV_{r} denoted by ℛp⊆Vp×Vp{\mathcal{R}}_{p}\subseteq V_{p}\times V_{p} and ℛr⊆Vr×Vr{\mathcal{R}}_{r}\subseteq V_{r}\times V_{r}. Nodes that are not merged with any other node form singleton equivalence classes. Denote with V¯o⊆Vo\overline{V}_{o}\subseteq V_{o} the set of object nodes to be pruned. Building nodes, robot node, and non-pruned object nodes are also treated as singleton equivalence classes. Let ℛ{\mathcal{R}} denote the resulting equivalence relation over V⁡(G)V(G). Then, the derived graph G′=κ⁡(G)G^{\prime}={\kappa}(G) has node set V⁡(G′)={[v]ℛ∣v∈V⁡(G)∖V¯o}V(G^{\prime})=\{[v]_{\mathcal{R}}\mid v\in V(G)\setminus\overline{V}_{o}\}. We identify each node in G′G^{\prime} with its equivalence class. Its edge set is obtained by mapping the endpoints of all edges not incident to pruned object nodes:

E(G′)={([u]ℛ,[v]ℛ)∣(u,v)∈E(G)∧u,v∉V¯o}.E(G^{\prime})=\{([u]_{\mathcal{R}},[v]_{\mathcal{R}})\mid(u,v)\in E(G)\land u,v\not\in\overline{V}_{o}\}.

Edge labels are inherited from the original relation that generated them and self-loops created by merging adjacent nodes are discarded. To ensure that the image of κ{\kappa} is a scene graph according to Definition 9 we require that

(vri,vpj)inc,(vrk,vpl)inc∈E⁡(G)∧(vpj,vpl)∈ℛp⟹(vri,vrk)∈ℛr.(v_{r_{i}},v_{p_{j}})_{\text{inc}},(v_{r_{k}},v_{p_{l}})_{\text{inc}}\in E(G)\land(v_{p_{j}},v_{p_{l}})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{p}\\ \implies(v_{r_{i}},v_{r_{k}})\in{\mathcal{R}}_{r}\kern 5.0pt. (3)

This condition ensures that each node has a unique parent connected with an inclusion edge. Second, for every equivalence class of place nodes induced by ℛp{\mathcal{R}}_{p}, the subgraph induced by that class under ℛadj{\mathcal{R}}_{\text{adj}} is connected. This ensures that each derived place node corresponds to a connected region of free configuration space.

Example 3 (Preimage of derived scene graph)

Given the environment ee from Example 1, we define 𝒢e{\mathcal{G}}_{e} as the set of all possible maximal scene graphs of ee. Let κe:𝒢e→𝒢der,e{\kappa}_{e}:{\mathcal{G}}_{e}\rightarrow{{\mathcal{G}}}_{{\text{der}},e} be a mapping from 𝒢e{\mathcal{G}}_{e} to a derived space 𝒢der,e{\mathcal{G}}_{{\text{der}},e} such that κe{\kappa}_{e}: merges all rooms into r123r_{123}; merges places p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} in p12p_{12}; merges places p3p_{3}, p4p_{4}, p5p_{5}, and p6p_{6} into p3456p_{3456}; and prunes the desk node dd, if present. Let the scene graph G1′∈𝒢der,eG^{\prime}_{1}\in{\mathcal{G}}_{{\text{der}},e}, shown in Fig. 2(a), be a derived scene graph under κe{\kappa}_{e}. When considering the preimage of G1′G^{\prime}_{1}, i.e., κe−1​(G1′)⊆𝒢e{\kappa}_{e}^{-1}(G^{\prime}_{1})\subseteq{\mathcal{G}}_{e}, we can determine, for example, that both G1G_{1} from Fig. 1(b) and G~1\tilde{G}_{1} from Fig. 2(b) are elements of κe−1​(G1′){\kappa}_{e}^{-1}(G^{\prime}_{1}) since κe​(G1)=κe​(G~1)=G1′{\kappa}_{e}(G_{1})={\kappa}_{e}(\tilde{G}_{1})=G^{\prime}_{1}. On the other hand, none of the graphs from Example 2 is in κe−1​(G1′){\kappa}_{e}^{-1}(G^{\prime}_{1}), due to aa being in p1p_{1} in G2G_{2}, G3G_{3}, or mm in p6p_{6} in G4G_{4}, G5G_{5}.

The action set U⁡(𝒢der)U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}) is the set of actions according to Definition 11, meaning that they are parametrized by the nodes of V⁡(𝒢der)V({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}). Because κ{\kappa} modifies the nodes of the scene graphs in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, U⁡(𝒢der)≠U⁡(𝒢)U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}})\not=U({\mathcal{G}}). To illustrate this issue, suppose under κ{\kappa}, an object node vov_{o} was pruned. Then, 𝚙𝚒𝚌𝚔(vo)\pick(v_{o}), 𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚌𝚎𝚘𝚗(vo,⋅)\placeon(v_{o},\cdot), 𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚌𝚎𝚘𝚗(⋅,vo)∉U⁡(𝒢der)\placeon(\cdot,v_{o})\notin U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}). Similarly, 𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(vp)∉U⁡(𝒢der)\moveto(v_{p})\notin U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}) if vp∉V⁡(𝒢der)v_{p}\notin V({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}) due to merging. Every derived action is interpreted as a motion primitive (Sec. III-D) over the maximal system. Whereas a motion primitive 𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(⋅)\moveto(\cdot) may correspond to a sequence in U⁡(𝒢)U({\mathcal{G}}) of length greater than one, retained 𝚙𝚒𝚌𝚔(⋅)\pick(\cdot) and 𝚙𝚕𝚊𝚌𝚎𝚘𝚗(⋅)\placeon(\cdot) actions correspond to sequences of length one.

For a maximal scene graph G1G_{1}, let pi{p_{i}} denote the place node containing the robot in GiG_{i}, i.e.,, (pi,va)inc∈E⁡(Gi)({p_{i}},v_{a})_{\text{inc}}\in E(G_{i}). Consider a motion primitive 𝚖𝚘𝚟𝚎𝚝𝚘(ω)\moveto(\omega), in which ω∈Vp/ℛp\omega\in V_{p}/{\mathcal{R}}_{p} and VpV_{p} is the set of place nodes in the maximal scene graph. Its induced trace (G1,u1,…,uN−1,GN)(G_{1},u_{1},\dots,u_{N-1},G_{N}) in the maximal system satisfies that every uiu_{i} is a move action over 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} and that pN∈ωp_{N}\in\omega. Furthermore, there exists an index m∈{0,…,N}m\in\{0,\dots,N\} such that pi∈[p1]ℛpp_{i}\in[p_{1}]_{{\mathcal{R}}_{p}} for all i<mi<m and pi∈ωp_{i}\in\omega for all i≥mi\geq m. Therefore, the robot remains inside the initial equivalence class until it enters the target class, and once it enters the target class it does not leave it.

Definition 12 (Derived scene graph transition system)

Given a scene graph transition system (𝒢,U⁡(𝒢),f)({\mathcal{G}},U({\mathcal{G}}),f), and a mapping κ:𝒢→𝒢der{\kappa}:{\mathcal{G}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}, let U⁡(𝒢der)U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}) be the set of actions over 𝒢der{\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}} according to Definition 11. Then, a scene graph transition system derived from (𝒢,U⁡(𝒢),f)({\mathcal{G}},U({\mathcal{G}}),f) by κ{\kappa} is the quotient system (𝒢der,U(𝒢der),ℱder):=(𝒢,U(𝒢der),⋄f)/κ({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}},U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}),{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{der}}):=({\mathcal{G}},U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}),\diamond_{f})/{\kappa}.

Note that (𝒢der,U⁡(𝒢der),ℱder)({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}},U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}),{\mathcal{F}}_{\text{der}}) is deterministic if κ{\kappa} is sufficient with respect to ⋄f\diamond_{f}, i.e., it satisfies (1).

V-B Scene graphs sufficient for planning

In Sec. III, we formally defined a model sufficient for planning for a task. Here, we apply this notion to the case when models are derived scene graph transition systems.

Let 𝒳=(𝒢,U⁡(𝒢),f){\mathcal{X}}=({\mathcal{G}},U({\mathcal{G}}),f) be the maximal scene graph transition system and T⊆Ω𝒳T\subseteq\Omega_{\mathcal{X}} be a task over its traces. Given an I-map κ:𝒢→𝒢der{\kappa}:{\mathcal{G}}\rightarrow{\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}, let 𝒳U⁡(𝒢der):=(𝒢,U(𝒢der),⋄f){\mathcal{X}}_{U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}})}:=({\mathcal{G}},U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}),\diamond_{f}) be the restriction of 𝒳{\mathcal{X}} by the set U⁡(𝒢der)U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}}) of motion primitives. Consecutively, let 𝒳der{\mathcal{X}}_{\text{der}} be the derived scene graph transition system, that is, 𝒳der:=𝒳U⁡(𝒢der)/κ{\mathcal{X}}_{\text{der}}:={\mathcal{X}}_{U({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}})}/{\kappa}.

Following Sec. III-D, the motion-primitive condenser is cMP:Ω¯𝒳U​(𝒢der)→Ω𝒳U​(𝒢der)c_{\text{MP}}:\bar{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{U}({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}})}\rightarrow{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{U}({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}})}. The I-map κ{\kappa} induces the condenser cκ:Ω𝒳U​(𝒢der)→Ω𝒳derc_{\kappa}:{\Omega}_{{\mathcal{X}}_{U}({\mathcal{G}}_{\text{der}})}\rightarrow\Omega_{{\mathcal{X}}_{\text{der}}} from the traces corresponding to motion-primitives to derived scene graph traces as given in (2). Then, the complete condenser is c=cκ∘cMPc=c_{\kappa}\circ c_{\text{MP}}.

Proposition 2

The following example illustrates the notions of sufficient scene graphs and when the required conditions are violated.

VI Discussion and Conclusions

We introduced a formal notion of sufficient scene graphs for robotic task planning. The proposed formalism reframes scene graph compression as a task-dependent information-abstraction problem. Rather than asking whether a derived scene graph preserves all properties of the maximal graph, the relevant question is whether it preserves the information needed to find plans that remain feasible in the original system. In this view, scene graphs are states of a transition system over which pruning and merging operations define an I-map, and derived scene graphs are quotient models induced by that mapping.

The resulting conditions separate distinct sources that allow checking feasibility of plans obtained over derived scene graphs. Deterministic quotient behavior ensures that derived actions have well-defined effects, while well-posedness ensures that task satisfaction is determined by derived traces. Together, these conditions guarantee that plans obtained over derived systems lift to feasible plans over the maximal system. Preservation of plan existence additionally requires completeness of the motion primitives induced by the derived action set.

This perspective is complementary to existing scene graph planning methods. Hierarchical, heuristic, and LLM-guided compression methods can be seen as implicitly choosing an I-map, and the framework presented here provides criteria for analyzing such choices. The characterization of planning sufficiency also suggests computational directions. Given a candidate merge and prune operations, sufficiency can be checked by searching counterexamples (similar to [27]), that is, searching for traces in the maximal system that map to the same derived trace but have different task labels. Furthermore, it also connects to partition-refinement methods for computing quotient systems since the induced I-map labeling is required to be a refinement of task labeling.

The present formulation is limited to deterministic scene graph transition systems, open-loop plans, and a restricted set of relations. Extending the framework to uncertainty, richer semantic relations, and developing algorithms for constructing (near) minimal sufficient derived scene graphs or their approximations remain important directions for future work.
